title: Title: I vibe coded a game in 10 days — then Google Play’s 12-tester / 14-day rule took longer than the whole build
author: Horror-Woodpecker686
selftext:
“Vibe coded” is the honest hook, but not the whole story. I made all the art myself (Gemini for the base, then way too long in paint.net cleaning it up) and did the balancing by hand. Claude wrote the code while I steered it pretty hard — more like pair programming with someone who types insanely fast and is occasionally very confidently wrong.

The thing I built is a small satirical economy sim: you start unemployed and work the German welfare system to get rich — fake job applications, cash-in-hand work, a casino to launder money, a loan shark, a villa you definitely can’t afford — while keeping your risk down so you don’t get raided and jailed. It’s an isometric 2D web game (Phaser), wrapped for Android.

Where Claude genuinely shined: all the systems and grind work. The whole economy loop, the welfare rules, the risk/raid mechanic, save/load, sound, and translating the entire UI into two languages — stuff that would’ve taken me weeks, done in an afternoon each. For logic and text it’s ridiculously good.

Where it drove me up the wall: anything visual. The worst was isometric depth sorting — the “player should walk *behind* the building but *in front of* the sidewalk” problem. We went in circles for days, fixed in front and broken in back, over and over. What finally worked was me literally painting the buildings in two colors in paint.net so it could tell foreground from ground. Lesson learned: when the problem is visual, stop typing prompts and just show it the answer. Honestly, if I did this again I’d use a real engine like Godot — a proper 3D scene gives you all that depth stuff for free, and I fought my flat web canvas the entire way.

But none of that was the real pain. **The real boss was Google Play.** The build took \~10 days. Getting it published took longer, because new dev accounts now have to run a closed test with 12 testers for 14 straight days before you’re even allowed to go live. I grabbed 20 testers to be safe — which, plot twist, meant I then had to test 20 other people’s apps in return, opening every single one every day. So for two weeks my “launch” was a finished game sitting idle while I did daily chores in 20 strangers’ apps.

One thing I’m convinced saved me: I kept pushing updates the entire test period, almost daily. Meanwhile I watched other devs with genuinely good apps stuck on their *third* round, failing again and again. My gut says a static build just sitting there looks dead, and constant updates make it look like a real, active project. Can’t prove it, but I passed first try while polished-but-static apps kept getting bounced. If you’re about to do this: line up your testers *before* you think you’re done, and don’t stop shipping during the test.

It’s live now. Happy to answer anything about the Claude workflow or the testing grind — and I’ll drop the link in a comment so this doesn’t read like an ad.

comments.author: slugger1
comments.body:
>I made all the art myself (Gemini for the base, then way too long in [paint.net](http://paint.net) cleaning it up)  

So gemini made the art and you cleaned it up?

replies.author: Horror-Woodpecker686
replies.body: I asked it to make a picture of a certain style of building with white or green background. So Claude could cut it out and make the background transparent.

replies.author: Horror-Woodpecker686
replies.body: I understand the logic of getting to a better app via testing. and I did some valuable feedback. But who has 12-20 people who test for them? From my Facebook „friends“ not a single one tested the app. Well, most are on iPhones anyway. And at the end you wasted hours opening apps you don’t care about and 20 other people did the same. And that is reality. I highly doubt that more than 10% of people manage to get through the test with „real“ testers who are genuinely interested in the app. Which is understandable. You have no idea what crap I had to look at for 14 days 🤪

replies.author: slugger1
replies.body:
Apples process is more straightforward and generally faster, but they also protect themselves with the $100 developer fee. On top of that, you usually have to deal with Swift, which I personally really do not like. When you ask your AI to generate an image for you, the keyword you are looking for is "chroma key". Usually a magenta or green background, which makes it much easier to remove the background afterward because of the strong color contrast.

It is kind of sad that people just open each other’s "trash" apps in circles to get through Googles screening process. Imagine if you and 19 other people had actually built meaningful apps and could give each other useful feedback on gameplay, usability, bugs, and overall quality instead. That would make the whole testing requirement a lot more valuable - as intented by google...

And now you might think, "but I made a cool game that is way better than all the garbage I had to test." But maybe every single one of those other developers thought exactly the same thing about their own app.

replies.author: Horror-Woodpecker686
replies.body: There is truth in that 😂. Well some of the apps were actually good and I’m still in contact with some of the developers on Facebook. And yes, I got feedback from them and I gave them. With the ones of the crappy apps it was as you described. Just get through testing phase by any means

replies.author: Horror-Woodpecker686
replies.body: By the way Apple‘s process seems to be more straight forward. They have real people looking at the app and give you feedback why you get rejected. Well, it also costs you 100 bucks per year to get a dev account vs something like 35 lifetime for Android. But google process is simply a black box for anyone.

comments.author: KhaosPT
comments.body:
I was curious so played a bit, it's nowhere near prime time... 
No settings on main menu to disable music, only in game.
Requires double tapping which is not really intuitive for mobile. At least give a notice.
You need some sort of idle animation.
Burglar came to me but nothing happens 
No responsiveness in general. I go to the job office take a ticket, go in my turn, do an application, nothing confirms if it worked or not, bad UI design
Same for the other activities.

replies.author: Horror-Woodpecker686
replies.body:
Actually agree. Was also most of the feedback, and it is already better than before. I simply wanted it to be finished finally. 🤪 This is a pure vanity project to see if I can launch a game without ever having written a line of code or done something like that before. Sort of got hooked now though and next one will be better. Well, also simple. Sozialbetrug is very complex and who plays difficult games nowadays. Monkey island would be a fail today, as it would be too frustrating for people to not get their dopamine in seconds.   
Next game will be a Diablo style western shooter. At least people can collect items from chests there.
